title: Emotional Intelligence for Daily Life
subtitle: Recognise and manage your emotions, understand other people, and handle family, work and community situations with calm and confidence.
description: A practical course built on recognised emotional intelligence models from Mayer and Salovey, Daniel Goleman and John Gottman. You will learn to name your feelings, calm yourself in heated moments, carry stress and grief, listen with real empathy, coach your children through big emotions, and apply these skills in marriage, business and community leadership.
outcomes: Name your emotions precisely using the Mood Meter and spot your personal triggers
Calm yourself in the moment with STOP, box breathing and grounding
Express anger and needs safely using 'I' statements and gentle start-ups
Listen with empathy and read emotional cues with cultural awareness
Coach children through strong feelings and handle conflict at home, work and in groups
Follow a personal 30-day plan to keep growing your emotional intelligence
audience: Women who want calmer homes, stronger relationships and steadier work lives, with no prior study of psychology needed.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a notes app on your phone
One or two trusted people to practise with

modules.title: Understanding Emotions
modules.overview: Start with what emotional intelligence really is, according to the researchers who named it. You will learn to put precise names to your feelings, see how a feeling turns into an action, and map the people, places and situations that set you off.

lessons.title: What emotional intelligence is (and what it is not)
objectives: Explain emotional intelligence in your own words
Name the four abilities in the Mayer and Salovey model
Describe Goleman's five areas of emotional intelligence
Correct three common myths about being emotionally intelligent

blocks.text: **Emotional intelligence** (often shortened to EI or EQ) is the ability to notice emotions in yourself and others, understand what they are telling you, and use that information to guide what you think, say and do. It is not about being soft, and it is not about never getting angry. It is about handling feelings well, so that they help you instead of controlling you.

blocks.name: processing-thoughts
blocks.alt: A woman thinking through her thoughts and feelings
blocks.caption: Emotional intelligence begins with pausing long enough to notice what you are feeling.

blocks.text: Where the idea comes from

The term was set out in a scientific paper in 1990 by two psychologists, **Peter Salovey** (Yale University) and **John Mayer** (University of New Hampshire). In 1995 the journalist and psychologist **Daniel Goleman** wrote the best-selling book *Emotional Intelligence*, which made the idea famous around the world. You will see both models in this course, because they help in different ways.
Model 1: Mayer and Salovey's four abilities
Mayer and Salovey describe emotional intelligence as four connected abilities. Think of them as steps that build on each other.

head: Ability
What it means
Everyday example
rows: Noticing feelings in faces, voices, bodies and in yourself
You see your daughter's shoulders drop when she comes home from school
You do your accounts in the morning when you feel fresh and focused
Knowing what causes a feeling and how it can change
You know your irritation is really tiredness after a long market day
Calming, lifting or redirecting feelings, in yourself and others
You take a short walk before replying to a hurtful message

blocks.text: Model 2: Goleman's five areas
Goleman, writing for leaders and workplaces, groups emotional intelligence into five areas. The first three are about you; the last two are about other people.

blocks.title: Goleman's five areas of EI
items: Social skills
Empathy
Motivation
Self-regulation
Self-awareness
blocks.caption: Self-awareness is the foundation; the other areas build on knowing yourself.

items: **Self-awareness:** knowing what you feel and why, and how it affects others.
**Self-regulation:** controlling sudden impulses and thinking before acting.
**Motivation:** working towards goals for reasons that matter to you, and keeping going after setbacks.
**Empathy:** understanding other people's feelings and points of view.
**Social skills:** building relationships, handling conflict and working well in groups.

blocks.text: Three myths to drop

items: **Myth: emotionally intelligent people are always calm and smiling.** Truth: they still feel anger, fear and sadness. They simply notice these feelings earlier and choose what to do with them.
**Myth: you are born with it or you are not.** Truth: these are skills. Like learning to drive or to sew, they improve with practice.
**Myth: emotional intelligence means pleasing everyone.** Truth: it includes saying no clearly and setting boundaries without shouting or sulking.

blocks.title: Worked example: the same morning, two ways
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Onitsha and has three children. One school morning the generator will not start, the children are late, and a supplier calls to say her goods will come two days late.
steps: Without EI: she shouts at her eldest son for being slow, snaps at the supplier, and spends the morning upset and short with customers.
With EI, step 1 (perceive): she notices her jaw is tight and her voice is rising.
Step 2 (understand): she tells herself, 'I am stressed because three things went wrong at once, not because my son is bad.'
Step 3 (manage): she takes three slow breaths, asks her son to help his sisters, and tells the supplier calmly that she needs a firm new date by 12 noon.
Step 4 (use): she uses the push of urgency to call a second supplier as a backup.
blocks.result: The problems are the same, but with EI she protects her relationship with her son and her supplier, and she has a backup plan by midday.

blocks.title: This course is not therapy
blocks.text: Emotional intelligence skills help with everyday stress and relationships. They do not replace a doctor, counsellor or psychiatrist. If low mood, worry or anger is lasting for weeks, affecting sleep, eating or work, or you have thoughts of harming yourself or others, please speak to a health professional, a trusted faith leader or the nearest hospital.
In the rest of this module you will practise the first ability, **perceiving and naming emotions**, because every other skill depends on it.
What EI looks like in a Nigerian home and workplace

items: At home: noticing that a teenager's rudeness may be hiding worry about exams, and asking about it before punishing.
In marriage: telling your husband 'I felt left out when you decided alone' instead of refusing to talk for three days.
In business: staying polite and firm with a customer who is haggling aggressively, so you keep both your price and your reputation.
In church, mosque or community groups: helping two members who have quarrelled to hear each other out.
With yourself: recognising when you need rest, and taking it without guilt.

blocks.text: Notice that none of these require a university degree, money or special equipment. They require attention, a few practised techniques and the willingness to try again when you get it wrong. That is exactly what the next 15 lessons will give you, one small skill at a time.

takeaways: Emotional intelligence is noticing, understanding and wisely using emotions, in yourself and others.
Mayer and Salovey describe four abilities: perceive, use, understand, manage.
Goleman's five areas start with self-awareness and build to social skills.
EI is a learnable skill, not a fixed personality trait.

activity.title: Your starting point
steps: Write Goleman's five areas down the left side of a page in your notebook.
Next to each, give yourself a score from 1 (rarely) to 5 (almost always) for how often you show it.
For your lowest score, write one recent real situation where it showed.
Write one sentence: 'By the end of this course I want to handle ... better.'
activity.evidence: A dated notebook page with your five scores and your one-sentence goal (keep it to compare at the end).

lessons.title: Naming your emotions precisely
objectives: Use the Mood Meter to place a feeling by energy and pleasantness
Replace vague words like 'fine' or 'bad' with precise emotion words
Notice where emotions show up in your body
Explain why labelling a feeling helps you calm it

blocks.text: Many of us were raised to answer 'How are you?' with 'I'm fine' or 'Thank God'. That is polite, but inside it hides a lot. If you cannot name what you feel, you cannot manage it. This lesson gives you tools to name feelings accurately.

blocks.name: sorting-thoughts
blocks.alt: A woman sorting thoughts into groups
blocks.caption: Sorting a jumble of feelings into clear names is the first step to handling them.

blocks.text: Why naming helps

Psychiatrist **Dan Siegel** sums this up as **'name it to tame it'**. Brain-imaging research at UCLA led by Matthew Lieberman (published in 2007) found that when people put their feelings into words, activity in the amygdala, a part of the brain linked to alarm and fear, went down. In plain terms: saying 'I feel anxious' to yourself is not weakness; it is already a step towards calm.
The Mood Meter

The **Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence** uses a simple tool called the **Mood Meter** in its RULER programme. You ask two questions: **How much energy do I have?** (high or low) and **How pleasant does this feel?** (pleasant or unpleasant). The answers place you in one of four colour zones.

blocks.title: The Mood Meter: four zones
items: Red: high energy, unpleasant
Yellow: high energy, pleasant
Blue: low energy, unpleasant
Green: low energy, pleasant
blocks.caption: Ask about your energy and how pleasant you feel, and you land in one zone.

head: Zone
Example feeling words
rows: angry, anxious, frustrated, panicked, irritated, worried, jealous
excited, hopeful, proud, joyful, eager, inspired
sad, tired, lonely, disappointed, discouraged, hopeless, bored
calm, content, relaxed, grateful, peaceful, satisfied

blocks.text: No zone is bad. Red energy helps you rush a sick child to hospital. Blue feelings tell you that you have lost something that mattered. The aim is to know which zone you are in and whether it suits what you need to do next.
Go from vague to precise

Once you know your zone, look for the most exact word. 'Bad' could mean ashamed, lonely, guilty or overwhelmed, and each one needs a different response. Shame needs kindness to yourself; loneliness needs connection; being overwhelmed needs help or fewer tasks.

items: Pause and ask: how much energy do I have right now?
Ask: does this feel pleasant or unpleasant?
Pick your zone colour.
Choose the most exact word from that zone. If two fit, say both: 'disappointed and a bit embarrassed'.
Notice where you feel it in your body.

blocks.text: Listen to your body

Emotions show up in the body, often before you have words for them. Common signs include a tight chest or fast heartbeat (anxiety), a hot face or clenched fists (anger), a heavy body and slow movement (sadness), and loose shoulders with easy breathing (calm). Your own signs may differ. Learning them is like learning the warning lights on a car dashboard.

blocks.title: Worked example: unpacking 'I'm just tired'
blocks.context: For example, Aisha, a teacher in Kaduna, comes home and tells her husband she is 'just tired' and goes quiet all evening.
steps: Energy check: low. Pleasantness: unpleasant. Zone: blue.
She asks herself what else is there. She remembers the head teacher criticised her lesson in front of colleagues.
Exact words: 'humiliated' and 'discouraged', not only 'tired'.
Body: heavy chest, no appetite.
Now she knows what she needs: to talk it through with someone she trusts and plan how to ask the head teacher for private feedback next time.
blocks.result: Naming the real feelings turned a silent evening into a short honest talk with her husband and a clear plan for the next day.

blocks.title: Use your own languages
blocks.text: Many Nigerian languages have rich words for feelings. If a Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or Pidgin word fits better than an English one, use it. The goal is accuracy, not English.
Practise naming several times a day for a week. At first it feels slow. After a while you will start to notice feelings earlier, while they are still small.
Feelings often come mixed

You can feel two or more emotions at once. On the day your first child leaves for university you may feel proud (yellow), sad (blue) and worried about school fees (red) all together. Naming each part is more accurate than choosing one. It also stops you judging yourself: you are not 'confused', you are simply feeling several true things at the same time.

Some people find a **feelings wheel** helpful. One widely used version was created by Gloria Willcox in 1982. It places a few core feelings such as sad, mad, scared, joyful, peaceful and powerful in the centre, with more exact words spreading outwards. You can find free printable versions online and keep one on your phone.

blocks.title: A quick daily habit
blocks.text: When someone asks how you are and you answer 'fine', silently finish the sentence for yourself: 'Fine, but actually a bit anxious about rent.' You do not have to tell everyone, but you should tell yourself.

takeaways: 'Name it to tame it': putting a feeling into words helps calm it.
The Mood Meter uses energy and pleasantness to find your zone.
Precise words (ashamed, lonely, overwhelmed) point to precise solutions.
Your body often signals an emotion before your mind names it.

activity.title: Three-times-a-day mood check
steps: Set three phone reminders: morning, after lunch and evening.
At each reminder, note your zone colour and one or two exact feeling words.
Write one body sign you noticed and what was happening at the time.
Do this for 5 days.
On day 5, circle the zone you were in most often.
activity.evidence: A 5-day mood log (notebook page or phone note) with 15 entries and your most frequent zone circled.

lessons.title: How a feeling becomes an action
objectives: Trace the chain from situation to thought to feeling to action
Explain how your interpretation shapes your emotion
Spot a thought that is making a feeling stronger
Choose a different action at the point of choice

blocks.text: Emotions are not random. They are fast responses that prepare us to act. Fear prepares us to run or protect; anger prepares us to fight for something; sadness slows us down to recover. Understanding this chain helps you step in before a feeling turns into an action you regret.

blocks.name: thought-process
blocks.alt: A person following a chain of thoughts
blocks.caption: Between what happens and what you do, there is a chain you can learn to see.

blocks.text: The emotion chain

blocks.title: From event to action
items: Situation happens
Thought or interpretation
Feeling and body response
Urge to act
Action and result
blocks.caption: The thought you add to a situation strongly shapes what you feel and do.

blocks.text: The key link is the **thought or interpretation**. Psychologists call this **appraisal**: the meaning you give to what happened. Two people can face the same situation and feel very differently, because they interpret it differently. This idea is also at the heart of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a well-researched approach used by counsellors.

head: Situation
Interpretation
Feeling
Likely action
rows: Husband does not reply to your message for 3 hours
Husband does not reply to your message for 3 hours
'He is probably in a meeting or has no network'
'She may come back after comparing prices'

blocks.text: The urge is not the action

Every emotion comes with an **urge**: to shout, to hide, to cry, to eat, to check the phone again. An urge is not an order. Between the urge and the action there is a small gap. Emotional intelligence is the skill of widening that gap so you can choose. Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived Nazi concentration camps, wrote about the freedom to choose one's attitude even in terrible circumstances; this course builds on the same idea with daily practice.
Thoughts that pour fuel on the fire

items: **Mind-reading:** 'She thinks I am a failure.' (You do not actually know.)
**Always and never:** 'He never helps.' (Is it truly never?)
**Catastrophising:** 'If I lose this contract, my business is finished.'
**Labelling:** 'I am useless.' (One mistake does not make a person useless.)
**Should statements:** 'She should know I am tired.' (People cannot read minds.)

blocks.text: When you notice one of these, ask three questions: **What is the evidence? What else could explain this? What would I tell a friend who thought this?**

blocks.title: Worked example: the family WhatsApp group
blocks.context: For example, Funmi posts photos of her new tailoring shop on the family WhatsApp group. Two hours later, 14 people have seen it but only her aunt has replied.
steps: Situation: few replies to her post.
First thought: 'Nobody in this family supports me.' Feeling: hurt (blue zone), with an urge to leave the group.
She checks the evidence: it is a weekday afternoon; most of her cousins work; her aunt did reply warmly.
Other explanations: people saw it while busy and plan to reply later; some rarely reply to anything.
New thought: 'People are busy. My aunt is proud of me.' Feeling: a little disappointed but calm.
Action: she leaves the group as it is and personally sends the photos to two cousins who might need clothes made.
blocks.result: By evening she has 9 replies and one cousin has booked a fitting. Leaving the group in anger would have cost her that customer.

blocks.title: Do not argue yourself out of real problems
blocks.text: Checking your thoughts is not the same as pretending everything is fine. If someone really is treating you badly, the goal is to see it clearly and respond wisely, not to explain it away.
In the next lesson you will look at the situations that set off your strongest chains, so you can prepare for them in advance.
Emotions also have useful messages
Before you try to change a feeling, ask what it is trying to tell you. Each emotion carries information that can guide good action.

head: Emotion
Usual message
Helpful action
rows: Check the real risk, prepare, ask for help
A boundary or value has been crossed
I may have acted against my values
This matters and is good for me
Notice it, share it, do more of it

blocks.text: When the message is accurate, act on it. When the message is based on a fuel thought, check the thought first.

A useful habit is to say the chain out loud, or in your head, when you notice a strong urge: 'The situation is..., I am telling myself..., so I feel..., and I want to...'. Saying it slowly is often enough to widen the gap between urge and action by a few seconds, and a few seconds is usually all you need to choose better words.

takeaways: Situation, thought, feeling, urge, action: the chain can be interrupted.
Your interpretation (appraisal) strongly shapes your emotion.
An urge is not an order; you can widen the gap and choose.
Challenge 'fuel' thoughts with evidence, other explanations and a friend's view.

activity.title: Map one emotion chain
steps: Pick a recent moment when you reacted strongly.
Write the five links: situation, thought, feeling, urge, action.
Underline any 'fuel' thought (mind-reading, always/never, catastrophising, labelling, should).
Write two other ways you could have interpreted the situation.
Write the action you would choose next time.
activity.evidence: A written five-link chain with one alternative thought and a new chosen action.

lessons.title: Finding your triggers and patterns
objectives: Define an emotional trigger and give examples
Keep a simple trigger log for one week
Spot patterns in time, people, places and body states
Write a plan for your top trigger

blocks.text: A **trigger** is anything that sets off a strong emotional reaction, often bigger than the situation seems to deserve. Triggers can be words ('You are just like your mother'), tones of voice, situations (being kept waiting), places, dates, or body states such as hunger and tiredness. Knowing your triggers lets you prepare instead of being caught off guard.

blocks.name: personal-notes
blocks.alt: A woman writing in a personal notebook
blocks.caption: A trigger log turns surprise reactions into patterns you can plan for.

blocks.text: Why some things hit harder

Triggers often connect to something important to us: respect, fairness, safety, being valued, or an old hurt. If you grew up being compared to a sibling, a comment comparing you to a co-worker may sting much more than it would sting someone else. This is normal. The point is not to blame yourself but to understand yourself.
The HALT check

A simple check used in many self-help and recovery programmes is **HALT**: am I **H**ungry, **A**ngry, **L**onely or **T**ired? Any of these makes ordinary problems feel bigger. Many mothers who skip breakfast to get children to school find they are shortest-tempered by mid-morning. Sometimes the fix is a meal or a rest, not a difficult conversation.
Keep a trigger log
For one week, each time you have a strong reaction, write a short entry. Use a notebook or a private phone note.

head: Day and time
What happened
Who was there
Feeling (zone and word)
Strength 1-10
HALT?
What I did
rows: Children not ready, late for school run

blocks.title: The trigger pattern cycle
items: Trigger appears
Automatic reaction
Short-term relief
Regret or conflict
Trigger feels stronger
blocks.caption: Without awareness, each reaction makes the next trigger feel even stronger.

blocks.text: Look for patterns

items: **Time:** Are most entries in the morning rush or late evening?
**People:** Does one person appear again and again?
**Theme:** Are many triggers about feeling disrespected, or about money, or about being ignored?
**Body:** How often were you hungry or tired?

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing's week
blocks.context: For example, Blessing sells foodstuff at a market in Port Harcourt. She logs 11 strong reactions in one week.
steps: She counts: 6 of the 11 happened before 10am.
5 of those 6 entries were marked 'hungry'.
4 entries were about customers asking for credit, and the theme was feeling taken advantage of.
Plan for the morning: eat bread and akara or a boiled egg before leaving home, even if small.
Plan for credit: write a clear sign, 'No credit, thank you', and practise one calm sentence: 'Sorry, I don't give credit, but I can give you a smaller quantity for your money.'
blocks.result: The next week she logs 5 strong reactions instead of 11, and only 1 is about credit.

blocks.text: Write a trigger plan

items: Name the trigger: 'When I am kept waiting at the bank...'
Name your usual reaction: '...I become sharp with the staff.'
Plan ahead: 'I will go with a snack and something to read.'
Plan in the moment: 'I will notice my jaw tightening and take three slow breaths.'
Plan your words: 'Excuse me, please could you tell me roughly how long the wait is?'

blocks.title: When a trigger links to past trauma
blocks.text: If certain reminders bring back intense fear, flashbacks or panic connected to a frightening past experience, a trained counsellor, psychologist or doctor can help. You do not have to work through that alone with a notebook.
Positive patterns count too

Your log will also show moments that went well. If you handled a difficult customer calmly on Wednesday, write down what was different that day. Perhaps you had eaten, slept well or prayed before opening the shop. These are your **protective factors**, and you can plan to repeat them on purpose.

Share your patterns, if you wish, with one trusted person, such as a sister, friend or spouse. Tell them one trigger and how they can help, for example: 'If you see me getting sharp with the children in the morning, please remind me to eat something.' Many triggers become easier to handle when someone else knows about them and is on your side.
Review your log again after a month. Triggers can change as your life changes: a new job, a new baby or a move to a new city can bring new ones, and old ones can fade as you practise.

Finally, be patient with yourself. You will still react to triggers, especially when you are tired. Each time you notice a trigger, even after you have reacted, you are building the awareness that makes the next time easier. Progress looks like reacting a little less often, a little less strongly, and recovering a little faster.

takeaways: A trigger is anything that sets off a reaction bigger than the situation.
HALT: hunger, anger, loneliness and tiredness make everything feel worse.
A one-week trigger log reveals patterns in time, people and themes.
A written trigger plan prepares you before, during and after.

activity.title: One-week trigger log and plan
steps: Copy the trigger log table into your notebook or phone.
Log every strong reaction (strength 6 or more) for 7 days.
Count entries by time of day, person and HALT state.
Choose your top trigger and write a five-line trigger plan for it.
activity.evidence: Your completed 7-day trigger log with totals, plus a written trigger plan.

quiz.q: In the Mayer and Salovey model, which ability comes first and supports all the others?
quiz.explain: You must first notice an emotion (perceive it) before you can understand, use or manage it. Social skills belong to Goleman's model.

quiz.q: Kemi feels her heart racing and feels worried before a meeting with her bank. Where is she on the Mood Meter?
quiz.explain: Worry is high energy and unpleasant, which places it in the red zone.

quiz.q: Your sister has not returned your call in two days. You think, 'She does not care about me any more.' What kind of 'fuel' thought is this?
quiz.explain: You are assuming you know what she thinks without evidence. That is mind-reading. She may simply be busy.

quiz.q: Most of Halima's angry outbursts happen at 11am on days she skips breakfast. Which tool best explains this pattern?
quiz.explain: HALT asks whether you are hungry, angry, lonely or tired. Hunger is a clear pattern here.

quiz.q: According to this module, why does naming a feeling precisely help?
options: It makes the feeling disappear for ever
It helps calm the brain's alarm response and points to the right solution
It proves the other person is wrong
It replaces the need for professional help
quiz.explain: Labelling feelings is linked with reduced alarm activity in the brain, and precise words point to precise responses. It does not remove feelings or replace professional help.

modules.title: Managing Your Emotions
modules.overview: Learn practical, recognised techniques to calm yourself in the moment, handle anger and stress, carry sadness and grief, and recover after setbacks. Every technique can be done with no equipment, in a market stall, a kitchen or an office.

lessons.title: Self-regulation: respond instead of react
objectives: Explain 'flipping your lid' using the hand model of the brain
Use the STOP technique in a heated moment
Practise box breathing and the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise
Choose a regulation tool that fits a real situation

blocks.text: **Self-regulation** means managing your emotions and impulses so that your actions match your values, even when you are upset. A **reaction** is fast and automatic: a shout, a slammed door, an angry voice note sent at midnight. A **response** is chosen. This lesson gives you tools to move from reacting to responding.

blocks.name: meditating
blocks.alt: A woman sitting calmly with eyes closed
blocks.caption: A few slow breaths can bring your thinking brain back online.

blocks.text: Flipping your lid

Psychiatrist Dan Siegel uses a simple **hand model of the brain**. Hold up your hand and fold your thumb into your palm, then fold your fingers over the thumb. Your wrist and palm stand for the deeper brain areas that handle alarm and survival. Your thumb stands for the emotional centre. Your fingers stand for the front of the brain (the prefrontal cortex) that plans, reasons and calms. When we are very upset, it is as if the fingers lift up: we **'flip our lid'** and the calm, thinking part loses its grip. The tools below help you fold the fingers back down.
STOP: a four-second pause

blocks.title: The STOP technique
items: Stop what you are doing
Take a slow breath
Observe body and thoughts
Proceed with a choice
blocks.caption: STOP creates a short gap between the urge and the action.

blocks.text: STOP is a simple mindfulness tool. **Stop** (freeze your hands and mouth), **Take a breath** (one slow breath), **Observe** (what am I feeling, what am I about to do?) and **Proceed** (choose the action that fits your values). It takes less than ten seconds and you can do it in the middle of a conversation.
Box breathing

items: Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of 4.
Hold your breath gently for a count of 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of 4.
Hold empty for a count of 4.
Repeat 4 times. If holding feels uncomfortable, skip the holds and just make the out-breath longer than the in-breath.

blocks.text: Slow breathing, especially a long out-breath, activates the body's calming system and slows the heart rate. That is why it works quickly, whether you are about to address a meeting or about to shout at a child.
5-4-3-2-1 grounding

When worry is racing, bring your attention back to the present by naming: **5** things you can see, **4** things you can touch, **3** things you can hear, **2** things you can smell and **1** thing you can taste. In a market, that might be: tomatoes, a red umbrella, the scale, a customer's blue wrapper, a bus; your stool, the money pouch, a nylon bag, your wrapper; a hawker's call, a radio, a horn; pepper, fuel; the sweet in your mouth.

blocks.title: Worked example: the school fees call
blocks.context: For example, Chioma, a civil servant in Enugu, gets a call from her son's school at work: fees are overdue and he may be sent home tomorrow. Her face goes hot and she wants to call her husband and shout.
steps: Stop: she puts the phone face down and does not dial.
Takes a breath: 4 rounds of box breathing at her desk, about one minute.
Observes: 'I am scared and embarrassed (red zone). I am telling myself he forgot on purpose.'
Proceeds: she calls the bursar first and asks if she can pay half (for example, N60,000 of N120,000, approximate figures) today and the rest within two weeks.
Then she calls her husband: 'The school called about fees. I have arranged to pay half today. Can we sit down tonight and plan the rest?'
blocks.result: Her son stays in school, and the evening is a planning talk instead of a fight.

head: Situation
Good tool
Why
rows: Heart racing before a meeting or interview
Brings attention back to the present
Lets the body settle before you return

blocks.title: Practise when calm
blocks.text: These tools work best if you practise them when you are calm, for example box breathing for two minutes each morning. Then your body knows what to do when stress hits.
Repair when you slip

You will not always catch yourself. When you do react badly, repair quickly. Go back, own your part and name what you will do differently: 'I am sorry I shouted this morning. I was stressed about money, but that is not your fault. Next time I will take a breath before I speak.' Repair teaches children and adults that relationships can survive mistakes, and it shows you are serious about change. Self-regulation is not perfection; it is noticing sooner and recovering faster each time.

takeaways: A reaction is automatic; a response is chosen.
When we 'flip our lid', the thinking brain loses control for a while.
STOP, box breathing and 5-4-3-2-1 grounding bring the thinking brain back.
Practise the tools daily when calm so they work under stress.

activity.title: Seven-day regulation practice
steps: Every morning for 7 days, do 4 rounds of box breathing and tick a box in your notebook.
Use STOP at least once a day in a real moment of irritation.
Write one line after each STOP: what you felt, and what you chose to do.
On day 7, write which tool helped you most and why.
activity.evidence: A 7-day tick chart with at least 5 written STOP notes.

lessons.title: Handling anger, frustration and stress
objectives: Recognise the early warning signs of anger and stress in your body
Use time-outs and 'I' statements to express anger safely
Sort stressors into what you can control and what you cannot
Build a simple daily stress-care routine

blocks.text: Anger is a normal, healthy emotion. It tells you that something feels unfair or that a boundary has been crossed. The problem is not anger itself but what we do with it. The American Psychological Association describes three main approaches: **expressing** anger in an assertive, not aggressive, way; **suppressing** it and redirecting it; and **calming** yourself inside. Suppressing anger for a long time without dealing with it can turn into resentment, so the healthiest path is usually calm, honest expression.

blocks.name: anger-symbol
blocks.caption: Anger is a signal worth listening to, not a command you must obey.

blocks.text: Know your anger ladder
Anger usually climbs in steps. Catching it at the bottom is much easier than at the top.

head: Level
Body and mind signs
Best action
rows: Sighing, slight tension, 'here we go again'
Name it, breathe, speak early and calmly
Jaw tight, voice rising, thinking in 'always/never'
STOP, slow breathing, lower your voice on purpose
Hot face, fast heart, fists clenched, wanting to hurt with words
Leave the room safely; talk only after you are calm

blocks.text: The time-out, done properly

items: Agree the signal in advance with your spouse or family: for example, 'I need 20 minutes.'
Say it calmly and add when you will come back: 'I am too angry to talk well. Let us talk again at 8pm.'
Use the time to calm down: walk, wash your face, breathe, pray. Do not spend it rehearsing arguments.
Come back at the agreed time. A time-out that never ends becomes stonewalling.

blocks.text: Say it with an 'I' statement

An 'I' statement describes your feeling and need without attacking. The pattern is: **'I feel [emotion] when [specific behaviour], because [reason]. I would like [request].'** Compare 'You are so careless, you never lock the shop!' with 'I feel worried when the shop is left unlocked, because we could lose our stock. Please could you lock it and send me a text when you leave?'
Stress: sort what you can control

blocks.title: Control versus no control
items: I can control
I cannot control
blocks.caption: Put your energy into the left column and practise acceptance for the right.
left: How I speak to my children

blocks.text: Stress is the body's response to demands. Short bursts can help you meet a deadline. Long-term stress with no recovery can harm sleep, mood and health. The World Health Organization's free guide **'Doing What Matters in Times of Stress'** teaches skills such as grounding, unhooking from difficult thoughts, and acting on your values. It is available as a free download.

blocks.title: Worked example: the month-end squeeze
blocks.context: For example, Zainab, a hairdresser in Abuja, has rent due on Friday, two clients who have not paid, and a sick mother. She cannot sleep.
steps: She writes every worry on paper: 8 items.
She sorts them: 4 she can act on (call the two clients, ask her landlord for one week, book her mother a clinic visit, ask her sister to share the clinic costs).
4 she cannot control (fuel price, her mother's illness itself, the landlord's mood, a slow month).
She schedules the 4 actions: 2 calls at 9am, landlord at 11am, clinic booking at noon.
For the rest she does 5 minutes of slow breathing at night and reminds herself, 'I have done what I can today.'
blocks.result: By Thursday one client has paid N15,000 (approximate), the landlord agrees to 5 extra days, and her sister pays half of the clinic visit. She sleeps better because her worries have a plan.

blocks.title: When anger becomes dangerous
blocks.text: If you or someone at home is being hit, threatened or controlled, this is not an anger-management problem to fix with breathing. Your safety comes first: go to a safe place, contact trusted family, the police or an organisation that supports women. In Nigeria, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 makes domestic violence an offence.
A daily stress-care routine

items: **Sleep:** aim for a regular bedtime; put the phone away 30 minutes before.
**Move:** a 20-minute brisk walk, dancing or chores done briskly.
**Eat:** regular meals; avoid going long hours without food.
**Connect:** one real conversation a day with someone who cares about you.
**Pause:** two minutes of box breathing or quiet prayer, morning and night.

blocks.text: Watch also for **displaced anger**, when frustration from one place lands on someone else. A hard day with a rude customer can come out as shouting at the house help or the children. When you notice this, say so honestly: 'I am upset about something at the shop, not about you.' Naming it often lowers the heat for everyone in the room.

takeaways: Anger is a signal; express it assertively, not aggressively.
Catch anger low on the ladder; take a time-out at level 7 or above.
'I feel... when... because... I would like...' keeps conversations safe.
Act on what you control, accept what you cannot, and care for your body daily.

activity.title: Anger ladder and stress sort
steps: Write your own anger ladder: your personal body signs at levels 1-3, 4-6, 7-8 and 9-10.
Agree a time-out signal with one family member and write it down.
Write three current worries in two columns: can control / cannot control.
Turn one 'can control' item into an action with a day and time.
Write one 'I' statement you could use this week.
activity.evidence: Your written anger ladder, control sort with one scheduled action, and one 'I' statement.

lessons.title: Carrying sadness, grief and disappointment
objectives: Explain why sadness is a normal and useful emotion
Describe grief as a process that moves back and forth
Use practical self-care and support steps during loss
Recognise signs that professional help is needed

blocks.text: Sadness tells us we have lost something that mattered: a person, a hope, a relationship, a business, our health, or a plan for the future. Many women are taught to 'be strong' and carry on as if nothing happened. Being strong does not mean not feeling. Allowing sadness, and getting support, usually helps people recover better than pushing it down.

blocks.name: feeling-blue
blocks.alt: A woman sitting alone feeling sad
blocks.caption: Sadness is a natural response to loss, and it deserves care rather than shame.

blocks.text: Different kinds of loss

items: **Bereavement:** the death of a loved one.
**Disappointment:** a failed exam, a contract you did not win, a visa refused, a business that closed.
**Relationship loss:** separation, divorce, a friendship that ended, children moving away.
**Hidden losses:** miscarriage, infertility, loss of health or of a role, which others may not see or talk about.

blocks.text: Grief moves back and forth

You may have heard of the 'five stages of grief' (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance), first described by Elisabeth Kubler-Ross. Kubler-Ross herself later explained that these are not fixed steps in order. People can feel several at once, move back and forth, or skip some. Another well-known idea, the **Dual Process Model** by Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, describes healthy grieving as moving between two kinds of activity: facing the loss (crying, remembering, talking about the person) and restoring life (sorting finances, caring for children, returning to work). Both are normal, and switching between them is healthy.

blocks.title: Moving between loss and restoring
items: Facing the loss
Taking a break
Rebuilding daily life
Remembering again
blocks.caption: Healthy grief swings between facing the loss and getting on with life.

blocks.text: What helps

items: **Allow the feeling.** Set aside time to cry, pray or remember, instead of fighting it all day.
**Keep the basics.** Small meals, water, some sleep, a short walk. Grief is tiring for the body.
**Accept practical help.** Let people cook, watch children or run errands. Tell them exactly what helps.
**Talk to someone safe.** A friend, sister, faith leader or support group.
**Keep simple routines.** Waking time, prayers, one small task, so the day has shape.
**Delay big decisions** such as selling a house or moving, if you can, until the first wave has passed.

blocks.title: Worked example: after a business closes
blocks.context: For example, Grace ran a small restaurant in Ibadan for four years. After rent and food prices rose, she closed it. For weeks she stays in bed and tells friends, 'I am fine.'
steps: She names her feelings: grief, shame and fear about money (blue and red zones).
She allows them: 20 minutes each evening to write about what she misses and what she learned.
She keeps basics: a walk to the market every morning to buy food for the house.
She accepts help: her friend reviews her accounts with her and they find she can sell her freezer and chairs for about N450,000 (approximate).
After six weeks, when she feels steadier, she starts a small home-cooking order service through WhatsApp, using the lessons from the restaurant.
blocks.result: Grace still feels sad about the restaurant at times, but she is working again and the sadness no longer controls her day.

blocks.text: Supporting someone who is grieving

items: Say the person's name and share a memory; many grieving people want the person remembered.
Offer specific help: 'I will bring soup on Tuesday,' not 'Call me if you need anything.'
Avoid phrases that close the conversation, like 'At least...' or 'Stop crying, it is God's will.'
Keep checking in after the burial; loneliness often grows when visitors stop coming.

blocks.title: When to get professional help
blocks.text: Sadness after loss is normal. Please see a doctor, counsellor or mental health professional if low mood lasts most days for more than two weeks, if you cannot eat, sleep or care for yourself or your children, if you feel hopeless, or if you have any thoughts of harming yourself. If you feel unsafe right now, go to the nearest hospital emergency unit or tell someone close to you immediately.

Remember that disappointment, even without a death, can bring real grief. Not getting a job, a pregnancy that did not happen, or a child who chose a different path can all deserve the same gentleness. Give yourself permission to feel it without comparing your loss to anyone else's.

Faith, culture and family traditions can be a real comfort during grief: prayers, the gathering of relatives, songs and remembrance events. Use what helps you. At the same time, it is fine to tell relatives gently if some customs feel too heavy right now, or if you need quiet rather than visitors.

Grief also has no fixed timetable. Anniversaries, festive seasons and family events can bring strong waves of sadness even years later. Plan for these days: let someone know, keep the day lighter and include a small act of remembrance.

takeaways: Sadness signals loss and deserves care, not shame.
Grief does not follow neat stages; it moves back and forth.
Healthy grieving mixes facing the loss with rebuilding daily life.
Lasting hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm need professional help now.

activity.title: A gentle support plan
steps: Think of a loss or disappointment you have carried, recent or old.
Write three feeling words that describe it.
List two things you do that help you face it and two that help you rebuild daily life.
Write the names of two people you could talk to, and one specific thing each could help with.
Write where you would go for professional help if needed (clinic, hospital, counsellor).
activity.evidence: A one-page support plan with feelings, helpful actions, two named supporters and one professional option.

lessons.title: Building resilience to bounce back
objectives: Define resilience as a set of learnable skills
Identify your sources of support, meaning and strength
Reframe a setback using the three Ps
Make a personal resilience plan

blocks.text: **Resilience** is the ability to adapt and recover when life gets hard: a job loss, illness, a failed business, family conflict, or the daily pressure of rising prices. The American Psychological Association describes resilience not as a fixed trait but as something built from behaviours, thoughts and actions that anyone can learn. Resilient people still feel pain. They simply find ways to keep going and grow.

blocks.name: seedling
blocks.caption: Like a seedling pushing through soil, resilience grows a little at a time.

blocks.text: Four pillars of resilience
The APA guide on building resilience groups helpful practices into four areas. Here they are in everyday terms.

head: Pillar
What it means
Examples
rows: Having people you can lean on
Family, friends, women's groups, church or mosque, cooperative (esusu/ajo)
Caring for your body and mind
Sleep, food, movement, prayer or quiet time, avoiding alcohol as an escape
Accepting change, hopeful but realistic thinking, learning from the past
Helping others, goals for your children, faith, building your business

blocks.title: What holds up resilience
items: Bouncing back
Meaning and purpose
Healthy thinking
Wellness
Connection
blocks.caption: Strong relationships and self-care form the base that everything else rests on.

blocks.text: The three Ps: how you explain setbacks

Psychologist Martin Seligman, known for his work on optimism, found that how people explain bad events to themselves affects how quickly they recover. He described three patterns, often called the three Ps:

items: **Personal:** 'It is all my fault.' versus 'Several things caused this, including some I could not control.'
**Pervasive:** 'My whole life is ruined.' versus 'This affects one area; other parts of my life are still good.'
**Permanent:** 'It will always be like this.' versus 'This is hard now, and it will change.'

blocks.title: Worked example: the rejected loan
blocks.context: For example, Amaka applies for a N500,000 (approximate) business loan from a microfinance bank to buy a second sewing machine and is turned down.
steps: First thoughts: 'I am not good at business (personal). Nothing works for me (pervasive). I will never grow (permanent).'
Personal, reframed: she asks the loan officer why. The reason: no 6-month bank statement showing regular sales. That is fixable.
Pervasive, reframed: her customers are happy, her children are well, she has a supportive sister.
Permanent, reframed: 'If I put all my sales through my Moniepoint account for 6 months, I can reapply.'
Connection: she joins a weekly ajo contribution with 9 other traders as a second path to the money.
blocks.result: Six months later she has a clear sales record and her ajo payout is due. A setback became a plan with two routes.

blocks.text: Small daily habits that build resilience

items: **Three good things:** each night, write three things that went well and why. Seligman's research team tested this exercise.
**One small step:** when a problem feels huge, ask 'What is one thing I can do today?'
**Look after your body:** sleep, regular meals and movement make setbacks easier to carry.
**Help someone else:** helping others is one of the APA's suggested ways to build a sense of purpose.
**Remember past survival:** list hard times you have already come through and what got you through.

blocks.title: Resilience is not doing everything alone
blocks.text: Asking for help is part of resilience, not a failure of it. Women who carry a household often think they must manage everything. Sharing the load with family, friends, your cooperative or a professional is a strong choice.
Your resilience toolkit at a glance

head: When this happens
Try this
Pillar
rows: You feel alone with a problem
Call one person today and tell them honestly how you are
Protect one hour of sleep and one proper meal
Check the three Ps and write a fairer sentence
You feel there is no point
Write who you are doing this for and one goal for this month

blocks.text: Resilience also grows from **flexible coping**: knowing when to push forward and when to rest, when to solve a problem and when to accept something you cannot change. A trader who cannot afford new stock this month might focus on serving loyal customers well and saving a little each day, instead of borrowing at a high interest rate in panic. Choosing the response that fits the situation is itself a resilience skill.

Finally, notice that resilience is shared. Families, cooperatives and women's networks such as the WODDI Good Mother Network (WGMN) are sources of strength. When you support another woman through her setback, you also strengthen your own sense of connection and purpose.
Review your plan every few months. As you notice which tools help most, keep them close, for example as a note on your phone you can open on a hard day.

takeaways: Resilience is a set of learnable skills, not a fixed trait.
Connection, wellness, healthy thinking and meaning hold it up.
Check your explanations: personal, pervasive, permanent.
Small daily habits like 'three good things' build strength over time.

activity.title: My resilience plan
steps: Write the four pillars as headings.
Under each, list two things you already have or do.
Choose one current setback and reframe it using the three Ps.
Practise 'three good things' every night for 7 nights.
Write one past hard time you survived and what helped.
activity.evidence: A one-page resilience plan, a three-Ps reframe, and 7 nights of 'three good things' entries.

quiz.q: Ada feels her face getting hot as her teenage son talks back. What does STOP ask her to do first?
options: Explain calmly why he is wrong
Freeze her hands and mouth for a moment
quiz.explain: The S in STOP is Stop: pause before speaking or acting. Then she takes a breath, observes and proceeds with a choice.

quiz.q: Which 'I' statement follows the pattern taught in this module?
options: You always leave the kitchen dirty.
I feel frustrated when the plates are left in the sink overnight, because ants come in. Please could you wash them before bed?
If you cared about me, you would clean up.
quiz.explain: It names the feeling, the specific behaviour, the reason and a clear request, without attacking the person.

quiz.q: Zainab has 8 worries. According to the control sort, what should she do with 'fuel prices are rising'?
options: Spend the evening planning how to change fuel prices
Put it in the 'cannot control' column and focus her energy on her budget
Ask her husband to fix it
quiz.explain: Fuel prices are outside her control. She can control her own budget and spending, so energy goes there.

quiz.q: A friend's mother died three months ago. Some days she laughs at work, other days she cries. What does the Dual Process Model say about this?
options: She has skipped the stage of acceptance
Moving between facing the loss and rebuilding daily life is healthy
She needs to stop remembering her mother
quiz.explain: Stroebe and Schut describe healthy grief as moving back and forth between facing the loss and restoring daily life.

quiz.q: After a failed exam, Ifeoma says, 'Everything in my life is a failure.' Which of the three Ps is this?
quiz.explain: Pervasive means letting one setback spread to every area of life. Reframe: 'I failed this exam; other parts of my life are going well.'

modules.title: Understanding Others' Emotions
modules.overview: Turn your attention outward. You will learn what real empathy is (and how it differs from sympathy), how to read faces, voices and silences with care, how small daily habits protect relationships, and how to coach your children through their big feelings.

lessons.title: Empathy: seeing through someone else's eyes
objectives: Distinguish cognitive, emotional and compassionate empathy
Explain the difference between empathy and sympathy
Use reflective listening to show you understand
Avoid common responses that shut people down

blocks.text: **Empathy** is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings and point of view. It is one of Goleman's five areas and the bridge between managing yourself and relating well to others. Empathy does not mean agreeing with everything someone says or does. It means understanding their experience well enough to respond with care.

blocks.name: people-hugging
blocks.caption: Empathy says 'I am with you', even when you cannot fix the problem.

blocks.text: Three kinds of empathy
Psychologists Daniel Goleman and Paul Ekman describe three kinds of empathy. You need all three.

head: Type
What it is
Example
rows: Understanding how someone thinks and sees the situation
'She is worried her boss will think she is lazy.'
Feeling something of what they feel
Your own chest tightens as your friend describes her fear
Understanding, feeling and being moved to help
You offer to sit with her while she calls the hospital

blocks.text: Too little emotional empathy can make you seem cold. Too much, with no boundaries, can leave you drained, especially for nurses, teachers, carers and mothers. Compassionate empathy balances the two: you care, and you also stay steady enough to help.
Empathy versus sympathy

Researcher **Brené Brown** explains the difference in a short animated talk for the RSA. Sympathy looks down at someone from a distance ('Oh, poor you') and often tries to find a silver lining ('At least...'). Empathy climbs down into the hole with them: 'I know what it is like down here, and you are not alone.'

blocks.title: Sympathy or empathy?
items: Sympathy
Empathy
blocks.caption: Empathy connects; sympathy keeps a distance.

blocks.text: Reflective listening: show you understand

items: **Give full attention.** Put the phone face down. Turn your body towards the person.
**Listen for feelings and facts.** What happened? How do they feel about it?
**Reflect back.** 'So you have been doing the work of two people since Bisi left, and you feel exhausted and unappreciated.'
**Check.** 'Have I understood that right?'
**Ask before advising.** 'Would you like ideas, or do you mostly need to talk?'

blocks.title: Worked example: the friend who lost her job
blocks.context: For example, Halima tells her friend Joy on the phone that her company in Lagos has just laid off 20 staff, including her.
steps: Unhelpful response: 'At least you got a severance package. You will find another job, don't worry.'
Joy gives full attention: she steps away from the TV.
She reflects: 'Eight years there, and they told you by email. You must be shocked and worried about the children's fees.'
Halima says, 'Yes, and embarrassed. I don't know how to tell my mother.'
Joy asks: 'Do you want to think through what to say to her, or do you just need to vent tonight?' Halima chooses to vent tonight and plan tomorrow.
blocks.result: Halima feels understood, and the next day they draft her CV together. Joy helped more by listening first than by rushing to reassure.

blocks.text: Responses that block empathy

items: **Minimising:** 'It's not that serious.'
**One-upping:** 'You think that is bad? Let me tell you what happened to me.'
**Quick fixing:** jumping to advice before the person feels heard.
**Spiritual bypassing:** 'Just pray about it' as a way of ending the conversation. Prayer can be a real comfort; offer it alongside listening, not instead of it.

blocks.title: Empathy for people you disagree with
blocks.text: Try cognitive empathy with someone who annoys you, such as a demanding customer or in-law. Ask silently: 'What might she be worried about? What does she need?' You do not have to agree, but understanding her need often shows you a better way to respond.
Protect yourself from empathy fatigue

Women are often the people everyone brings their problems to: the sister who listens, the friend who advises, the mother who absorbs everyone's moods. Feeling other people's pain all day without rest can lead to exhaustion, sometimes called **empathy fatigue** or compassion fatigue, which is common among health workers and carers. Signs include feeling numb, irritable, or dreading other people's calls.

items: **Notice your limit:** 'I can listen for 15 minutes tonight, then I need to sleep.'
**Separate their feeling from yours:** 'This is her sadness. I can care without carrying it all.'
**Refill yourself:** rest, prayer, laughter and time with people who also listen to you.
**Share the load:** you do not have to be the only support. Encourage her to talk to others too, including professionals where needed.

blocks.text: Empathy is a strength that lasts longest when it is balanced with boundaries.
Like every skill in this course, empathy improves with practice. Start with one conversation a day where your only goal is to understand, not to fix or win.

takeaways: Cognitive, emotional and compassionate empathy work together.
Sympathy keeps a distance; empathy connects ('you are not alone').
Reflect feelings and facts, check, then ask before advising.
Avoid 'At least...', one-upping and quick fixes.

activity.title: Three reflective conversations
steps: Over the next 3 days, choose 3 conversations where someone shares a problem.
In each, reflect back the facts and one feeling before giving any advice.
Ask: 'Would you like ideas, or do you need to talk?'
Afterwards write what you said, how they responded, and one thing you would improve.
activity.evidence: Notes on 3 conversations, each with your reflective sentence and the person's response.

lessons.title: Reading faces, voices and silences
objectives: Notice facial, vocal and body cues of emotion
Interpret cues with cultural awareness and without jumping to conclusions
Read emotional cues in WhatsApp and phone communication
Check your reading with a gentle question

blocks.text: Much of what people feel is shown, not said. Tone of voice, facial expression, posture and even silence carry emotional messages. Reading these cues accurately is the first ability in the Mayer and Salovey model, applied to other people. It helps you respond to what someone really needs, not only to their words.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.caption: Watching the face and listening to the tone tells you more than words alone.

blocks.text: Three channels to watch

head: Channel
What to notice
Possible meanings
rows: Tight lips may show anger or holding back; a forced smile may hide hurt
Fast and loud may mean anxiety or anger; flat and slow may mean sadness or tiredness
Crossed arms may mean defensiveness or simply cold; turning away may mean discomfort

blocks.text: Psychologist Paul Ekman's research found some facial expressions of basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust, are recognised across many cultures. But how much people show, and in which situations, depends strongly on culture, family and personality.
Read cues in context

items: **Culture:** in many Nigerian families, a younger person avoids direct eye contact with an elder as a sign of respect, not dishonesty.
**Clusters, not single signs:** one crossed arm means little. Crossed arms, a short reply and looking away together tell you more.
**Change from normal:** notice when someone who is usually chatty goes quiet. A change from their usual pattern is often the strongest clue.
**Situation:** a sharp tone in a hot, crowded bus may be about the heat, not about you.

blocks.title: Before you decide what someone feels
items: Look at face, voice, body
Look for a cluster
Compare with their normal
Consider culture and situation
Ask gently to check
blocks.caption: A good reading is a guess you check, not a judgement.

blocks.text: Reading cues in messages

On WhatsApp and SMS you lose face and voice, so misreadings are common. A short 'Ok.' can feel cold, but the sender may just be busy or driving. Clues in messages include sudden changes in length, missing greetings when they normally greet, delayed replies compared with usual, and voice notes where you can hear tone. When a message worries you, call or send a voice note instead of guessing. Never assume the worst from punctuation alone.

blocks.title: Worked example: the quiet staff member
blocks.context: For example, Ronke runs a small catering business in Abeokuta with 4 staff. Usually her assistant, Tolu, jokes while cooking. For three days Tolu has been quiet, working fast, avoiding eye contact and leaving on time exactly.
steps: Cluster: quiet, avoiding eye contact, leaving promptly.
Change from normal: very different from her usual cheerful self.
Ronke avoids guessing ('She is lazy now' or 'She wants to quit').
She asks privately: 'Tolu, you have seemed quieter this week. Is everything okay? No pressure, I just noticed.'
Tolu shares that her mother is in hospital and she is rushing to visit after work.
blocks.result: Ronke allows her to leave 30 minutes early for two weeks. Tolu stays, and her loyalty to the business grows.

blocks.text: Check gently

Your reading is a guess. Check it with a tentative, open question that leaves room for the person to say no: 'You seem a bit tense, am I right?' or 'I may be wrong, but you sound disappointed.' Avoid accusing statements like 'Why are you angry with me?', which can make someone defensive even if they were not angry.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: Noticing someone's feelings does not give you the right to push. If they say 'I'm fine' after you have asked gently, accept it and let them know the door is open: 'Okay. If you want to talk later, I am here.'
Listening to what is not said

Silence can mean many things: thinking, respect, discomfort, sadness, anger, or simply tiredness. In many homes, a wife or daughter-in-law may stay silent to keep peace while feeling hurt inside. A child may go quiet rather than say they are being bullied. Do not treat silence as agreement. If something important was discussed and someone said nothing, follow up later in private: 'You were quiet when we talked about the move. What do you think about it?'

Also read your own cues. If you notice you are speaking fast, frowning or folding your arms, others are reading those signals too. A relaxed face, an open posture and a calm voice invite people to share. Before an important conversation, take a breath and soften your shoulders so your body says the same thing as your words.
With practice, reading cues becomes quicker and more accurate. Keep checking your guesses, and you will learn the particular signals of the people closest to you.

takeaways: Watch face, voice and body, and look for clusters of cues.
Changes from someone's normal behaviour are strong clues.
Culture and situation shape what cues mean.
Check your reading with a gentle question, and respect privacy.

activity.title: Cue-reading practice
steps: Choose one person you see daily. Write down their 'normal': voice, energy, how they greet you.
Over 3 days, note any change from normal and the cluster of cues you saw.
Check once with a gentle question.
Write what you guessed, what they said, and whether your guess was right.
activity.evidence: A short note comparing your guess with what the person actually told you.

lessons.title: Strengthening relationships with everyday EQ
objectives: Recognise and respond to 'bids' for connection
Name the Four Horsemen that damage relationships and their antidotes
Use a gentle start-up to raise a complaint
Make and accept repair attempts after conflict

blocks.text: Relationships with friends, siblings, in-laws, neighbours and colleagues are built in small moments. Psychologist **John Gottman** and his colleagues have studied couples and families for decades at what is now The Gottman Institute. Many of their findings apply to any close relationship, and they give us clear, practical habits.

blocks.name: true-friends
blocks.caption: Strong friendships are built from many small moments of attention.

blocks.text: Bids for connection

A **bid** is any attempt to get attention, interest or support: 'Look at this video,' 'My back is paining me,' a sigh, a touch. You can respond in three ways: **turn towards** (show interest), **turn away** (ignore, keep scrolling) or **turn against** (respond with irritation). Gottman's research found that people in lasting relationships turned towards each other's bids far more often than people whose relationships ended.
The Four Horsemen and their antidotes
Gottman named four communication patterns that strongly predict relationship breakdown, and he called them the Four Horsemen. Each has an antidote.

head: Horseman
What it sounds like
Antidote
What it sounds like
rows: 'You are so selfish, you never think of anyone.'
'I felt left out when you made plans without asking me. Can we plan together next time?'
Regularly say what you value and respect
'It's not my fault, you did worse!'
'You are right, I forgot. I'm sorry.'
Walking away, refusing to speak for days
'I'm overwhelmed. Give me 20 minutes and we will talk.'

blocks.text: Gottman identified **contempt** as the strongest predictor of breakup of the four. It communicates disgust and superiority. If you notice contempt in yourself, it is a sign you need to rebuild appreciation.

blocks.title: A gentle start-up
items: Start with 'I feel'
Describe the situation
Avoid blame words
State a positive need
blocks.caption: How a difficult conversation starts usually decides how it ends.

blocks.text: The 5 to 1 ratio

In Gottman's studies, stable couples had about **five positive interactions for every negative one** during conflict. Positive interactions include showing interest, a kind word, humour, affection and agreement. This does not mean avoiding all criticism. It means making sure warmth far outweighs tension.

blocks.title: Worked example: two sisters and the family business
blocks.context: For example, Ijeoma and her younger sister Nneka run a cosmetics stall together in Aba. Ijeoma is upset that Nneka arrives late most days.
steps: Old way (criticism): 'You are so unserious. You are always late and I do all the work.' Nneka becomes defensive and they argue in front of customers.
New way, gentle start-up, in private: 'I feel stressed when I open alone, because the morning rush is our busiest hour. Could you be here by 8am, or can we agree which days you open?'
Nneka explains she has been taking their mother to the clinic twice a week.
Ijeoma takes responsibility: 'I didn't know. I'm sorry I assumed.'
They agree: Nneka opens on Monday, Wednesday and Friday; Ijeoma on clinic days.
blocks.result: The problem is solved in ten minutes, and the sisters avoid a quarrel that could have damaged both the business and their relationship.

blocks.text: Repair attempts

A **repair attempt** is anything that stops tension from rising: a joke, a touch, 'Let me try again,' 'I see your point.' Every relationship has conflict. What matters most is whether repair attempts are made and accepted. When someone offers a repair, try to accept it, even if you are still a little upset.

blocks.title: When a relationship is harmful
blocks.text: These tools are for relationships where both people are basically safe and respectful. If someone repeatedly insults, threatens, controls or harms you, the problem is not your communication. Seek support from trusted people, a counsellor or an organisation that helps women.
Appreciation as a daily habit

Appreciation is the main antidote to contempt, and it works in every relationship. Make it specific: not just 'thank you', but 'thank you for picking the children up today, it gave me time to finish my orders.' Specific thanks show you noticed the effort. Try to catch people doing something right at least once a day: your spouse, a colleague, an apprentice, a child.

items: Send a short WhatsApp voice note to a friend saying one thing you value about her.
Tell a family member in front of others what they did well.
Thank a co-worker for a specific task, by name.
Notice small bids: put down your phone when someone starts talking to you.

blocks.text: Small moments add up. A relationship with many deposits of warmth can survive the withdrawals that conflict brings.

takeaways: Turn towards small bids for attention; they build trust.
Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling each have an antidote.
Start hard conversations gently: feeling, situation, positive need.
Aim for far more positive moments than negative ones, and accept repairs.

activity.title: Bids and gentle start-ups
steps: For 2 days, notice bids from one close person and tick each time you turned towards them.
Write down one complaint you have been holding in.
Rewrite it as a gentle start-up: I feel... when... could we...?
Have the conversation in private, and note how it went.
activity.evidence: Your bid tally and your written gentle start-up with a short note on the outcome.

lessons.title: Emotion coaching for mothers and caregivers
objectives: Describe the five steps of emotion coaching
Validate a child's feelings while still setting limits on behaviour
Help children name feelings at different ages
Look after your own emotions as a caregiver

blocks.text: Children are not born knowing how to manage feelings. They learn mostly from the adults around them: how we react when they cry, how we handle our own anger, and whether feelings are talked about at home. John Gottman's research with families, described in his book *Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child*, found that parents who coach children through emotions help them manage feelings and get along better with others.

blocks.name: motherhood
blocks.alt: A mother caring for her child
blocks.caption: Children learn to handle feelings by watching and being guided by the adults who care for them.

blocks.text: Feelings are allowed; some behaviour is not

The core idea of emotion coaching is simple: **all feelings are acceptable, but not all behaviour is.** A child may feel angry that his brother took his toy. Hitting is not allowed. When we punish the feeling ('Stop crying or I will give you something to cry about'), children learn to hide feelings rather than manage them. When we accept the feeling and guide the behaviour, they learn self-regulation.
The five steps of emotion coaching

blocks.title: Gottman's five steps
items: Notice the emotion
See a chance to connect
Listen and validate
Help name it
Set limits, solve problems
blocks.caption: Each step builds on the one before.

items: **Be aware of the child's emotion,** especially when it is still small.
**See it as a chance** to connect and teach, not as a nuisance.
**Listen with empathy and validate:** 'You are upset because you wanted to go with Daddy.'
**Help the child name the feeling:** 'Are you feeling disappointed? Jealous? Scared?'
**Set limits and solve the problem together:** 'It's okay to be angry, but we don't hit. What could you do next time your brother takes your toy?'

blocks.title: Worked example: the 6-year-old at the party
blocks.context: For example, Bukola takes her 6-year-old daughter, Dami, to a cousin's birthday. When the cake is cut, Dami screams and throws her plate because she did not get the piece with the candle.
steps: Notice: Bukola sees Dami's face crumple before the plate is thrown and kneels down to her level.
Connect: instead of shouting, she takes Dami's hand and moves her a few steps away from the crowd.
Validate: 'You really wanted the piece with the candle. That is disappointing.'
Name: 'Are you feeling disappointed and a bit jealous?' Dami nods, crying.
Limits and problem-solving: 'It is okay to feel disappointed. Throwing plates is not okay. Let's pick up the plate together. Next time, what can you do when you feel this way?' Dami says, 'Tell you.'
blocks.result: Dami calms in about 3 minutes, helps clean up and goes back to play. She has learned a word for her feeling and a better action, instead of only learning that she is 'bad'.

blocks.text: Feeling words by age

head: Age
What helps
rows: Simple words: happy, sad, angry, scared. Point to faces in picture books.
More words: disappointed, jealous, worried, proud, embarrassed. Use the Mood Meter colours.
Talk about causes: 'What made you feel left out?' Practise calming tools together.
Listen more than you lecture. Ask open questions. Respect their need for privacy.

blocks.text: Your emotions matter too

Caregivers cannot pour from an empty cup. Mothers, grandmothers and other carers often go without rest, help or time for themselves. Tiredness and stress make it much harder to stay calm with children. Use the tools from Module 2 on yourself: notice your HALT signs, take a breath before responding, share tasks with your partner or family, and repair if you shout.

blocks.title: Never use fear or harsh physical punishment to stop feelings
blocks.text: UNICEF and the World Health Organization recommend positive, non-violent discipline. If you are worried that a child's anger, fear or sadness is very intense, lasting a long time, or affecting school, eating or sleep, speak to a doctor or school counsellor. If you ever feel close to losing control with a child, put the child somewhere safe, step away, and call someone you trust.
Modelling: children copy what we do

Children learn as much from watching you manage your own feelings as from anything you say. When you are upset, you can narrate your coping out loud: 'Mummy is feeling frustrated because the light went off while I was cooking. I'm going to take three deep breaths and then light the gas.' This teaches them that adults have feelings too, and shows them exactly what to do.

When you lose your temper, repair with the child: 'I'm sorry I shouted. I was tired, but it was not your fault. I love you.' Some parents worry that apologising to a child weakens their authority. In practice, it teaches responsibility and makes children feel safe. Over time, children who are coached in this way begin to use the same words with their siblings and friends.

takeaways: All feelings are acceptable; not all behaviour is.
Emotion coaching: notice, connect, validate, name, set limits and solve problems.
Teach feeling words that fit the child's age.
Caregivers need care too: rest, support and repair after mistakes.

activity.title: Coach one big feeling
steps: Choose a child you care for (your own, a niece, nephew or grandchild).
The next time they show a strong emotion, use the five steps.
Write down the words you used for each step.
Teach them one new feeling word this week and notice if they use it.
Write one way you looked after your own emotions this week.
activity.evidence: A written five-step record of one coaching moment and the new feeling word you taught.

quiz.q: Your friend says her husband has lost his job. Which response shows empathy rather than sympathy?
options: At least he still has his health.
That sounds really frightening. How are you both coping?
My cousin lost his job too and it was worse.
Don't worry, God will provide another job soon.
quiz.explain: Empathy names the feeling and keeps the focus on her. 'At least...', one-upping and quick reassurance shut the conversation down.

quiz.q: Chiamaka's normally chatty colleague has been quiet all week. What is the best next step?
options: Assume she is angry with Chiamaka
Ignore it, it is not Chiamaka's business
Ask privately and gently: 'You seem quieter this week, is everything okay?'
Tell the manager the colleague has a bad attitude
quiz.explain: A change from normal is a strong clue. Check your reading with a gentle, private question and respect her answer.

quiz.q: During a quarrel, Emeka rolls his eyes and mocks the way his wife speaks. Which of the Four Horsemen is this?
quiz.explain: Mocking and eye-rolling show superiority and disgust. That is contempt, which Gottman found is the strongest predictor of breakup.

quiz.q: Which is a gentle start-up?
options: You never help with the children.
I feel overwhelmed at bedtime with three children. Could you bathe the two boys on weekdays?
quiz.explain: It starts with 'I feel', describes the situation without blame and states a clear positive need.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old kicks his sister after she breaks his toy. Following emotion coaching, what should his mother say?
options: Stop crying, it is only a toy.
You are a bad boy. Go to your room.
You are angry she broke your toy. It's okay to be angry, but kicking is not okay. Let's think what you can do instead.
Kick her back if she breaks your things.
quiz.explain: Emotion coaching validates the feeling, names it, sets a limit on the behaviour and solves the problem together.

modules.title: Applying EQ in Daily Life
modules.overview: Put everything together in the places where it matters most: your work or business, your marriage or partnership, your community and leadership roles, and your own ongoing growth. You finish with a 30-day plan to keep building your emotional intelligence.

lessons.title: EQ at work and in your business
objectives: Handle an upset customer using the LAST method
Give feedback to a staff member or colleague using the SBI model
Receive criticism without becoming defensive
Use emotional awareness to make better business decisions

blocks.text: Whether you work in an office, a school, a hospital, or run your own stall, salon or online shop, work is full of emotions: pressure from bosses, demanding customers, difficult colleagues, money worries. Goleman's original writing on emotional intelligence focused on the workplace, arguing that self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social skills matter alongside technical skill, especially for people who lead others.

blocks.name: happy-customer
blocks.alt: A smiling customer at a shop
blocks.caption: Customers remember how you made them feel, especially when something went wrong.

blocks.text: Handling an upset customer: LAST
**LAST** is a simple service-recovery method used in hospitality and customer service: **Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank.**

blocks.title: The LAST method
items: Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve the problem
Thank the customer
blocks.caption: Calming the feeling first makes solving the problem much easier.

items: **Listen** without interrupting. Let the customer finish. Nod, keep a calm face, and reflect: 'So the gown was not ready on Saturday as promised, and you had to wear something else to the wedding.'
**Apologise** for their experience, sincerely and without excuses: 'I am truly sorry. That must have been very frustrating.'
**Solve:** offer a clear fix or choice: 'I can finish it today by 5pm and give you N3,000 (approximate) off, or refund your deposit. Which do you prefer?'
**Thank** them: 'Thank you for telling me directly. It helps me improve.'

blocks.title: Worked example: the angry online order
blocks.context: For example, Patience sells hair products on Instagram from Benin City. A customer sends an angry voice note: her order of 3 bottles of hair oil (about N12,000 total, approximate) arrived with one bottle broken, and she calls Patience 'a scammer'.
steps: Patience feels insulted (red zone). She uses STOP and waits 10 minutes before replying.
Listen: she replies, 'I hear you. You paid for 3 bottles and one arrived broken. That is very disappointing.'
Apologise: 'I am sorry this happened.' She does not argue about the word 'scammer'.
