Solve: 'Please send me a photo of the broken bottle. I will send a replacement with my rider tomorrow at no cost, and I will pack in bubble wrap from now on.'
Thank: 'Thank you for letting me know quickly.'
blocks.result: The replacement costs her about N4,000 plus delivery (approximate). The customer leaves a positive review and orders again the next month.

blocks.text: Giving feedback: the SBI model

The **Situation, Behaviour, Impact (SBI)** model, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, keeps feedback specific and fair. Describe the **situation** (when and where), the **behaviour** (what the person did, not your judgement of them), and the **impact** (the effect). Then invite their view.

head: Unhelpful
SBI version
rows: 'At the shop on Tuesday afternoon (S), when the woman asked about prices, you kept looking at your phone (B). She left without buying, and we may have lost a regular customer (I). What happened?'
'In this morning's meeting (S), you explained the new price list clearly (B). Everyone understood and there were no questions afterwards (I). Thank you.'

blocks.text: Receiving criticism

items: Breathe and listen to the end before responding.
Ask for specifics: 'Can you give me an example?'
Separate the message from the delivery. Even if it was said harshly, is there something useful in it?
Thank the person, and take time to think if you need it: 'Let me reflect on that and come back to you tomorrow.'

blocks.text: Emotions and business decisions

Strong emotions can push poor decisions: panic-buying stock when prices rise, saying yes to every credit request out of guilt, or making a big investment because a friend made you feel excited. Before any decision involving significant money, check your zone. If you are in the red or very high yellow zone, wait 24 hours, write down the numbers and, if possible, talk to someone you trust.

blocks.title: Scams play on emotions
blocks.text: Many scams are designed to make you feel fear ('Your account will be blocked'), greed ('Double your money in 7 days') or urgency ('Pay now or lose the offer'). A strong rush of emotion around money is a signal to slow down. Never share your BVN, card PIN or OTP with anyone who contacts you, and check directly with your bank using the official number.

Your own wellbeing at work matters too. If you notice you are dreading work every day, feeling exhausted even after rest, or becoming cynical about customers or colleagues, these can be signs of burnout. Talk to your manager about workload if you are employed, share tasks or close one day a week if you run your own business, and see a doctor if the exhaustion continues.

takeaways: LAST: listen, apologise, solve, thank, to calm and keep customers.
SBI feedback: situation, behaviour, impact, then ask for their view.
Receive criticism by listening fully and asking for specifics.
Strong emotions around money are a signal to slow down, especially with possible scams.

activity.title: Work EQ practice
steps: Write a LAST script for a complaint you often get at work or in your business.
Write one piece of positive SBI feedback and deliver it to a colleague, staff member or apprentice this week.
Recall the last time you were criticised and write how you would respond using the four tips.
Write one money decision you made in a strong emotion and what you would do differently.
activity.evidence: Your LAST script, one delivered SBI feedback with the person's reaction, and a short reflection.

lessons.title: EQ in marriage and partnership
objectives: Use 'love maps' to deepen understanding of your partner
Handle conflict using a gentle start-up, breaks and compromise
Tell solvable problems from ongoing differences
Recognise when outside help or safety steps are needed

blocks.text: Marriage and long-term partnership bring two people, often two families, and sometimes two cultures together. Money, children, in-laws, roles at home and faith can all become sources of tension. Emotional intelligence will not remove disagreement, but it changes how couples move through it. Many of the most practical ideas come from John Gottman's research with couples, introduced in Module 3.

blocks.name: couple
blocks.caption: Small daily habits of attention and respect protect a marriage through hard seasons.

blocks.text: Love maps: know your partner's world

Gottman uses the term **love map** for how well you know your partner's inner world: their worries, hopes, friends, stresses at work and dreams. Couples with detailed love maps cope better with stressful events like a new baby or a job loss. You build a love map by asking open questions and remembering the answers.

items: 'What is worrying you most at work right now?'
'If money were not a problem, what would you love to do?'
'What was the best part of your week?'
'Is there anything I do that makes you feel really appreciated?'

blocks.text: Handling conflict well

blocks.title: Healthy conflict checklist
items: Choose a calm time
Start gently
Take breaks if flooded
Accept repair attempts
Look for compromise
blocks.caption: These five habits keep disagreements from turning into lasting damage.

blocks.text: Gottman describes **flooding**: when your heart is racing and you feel overwhelmed, you cannot listen well. If either of you is flooded, take a break of at least 20 minutes, calm your body, and come back. Do not use the break to plan your next attack.
Solvable problems and lasting differences

Gottman's research found that a large share of couple conflicts are about **perpetual problems**: ongoing differences in personality, values or habits that may never fully go away. One may be a saver and one a spender; one may want to visit family every weekend and the other prefer rest. The goal with these is not to 'win', but to understand the dream or need behind each position and find a way to live with the difference. **Solvable problems**, like who takes the children to school on Mondays, can be fixed with a clear agreement.

blocks.title: Worked example: money and the extended family
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze and her husband Tunde both work in Lagos. Tunde regularly sends money to his younger brothers, and Adaeze feels the household is being left short. They argue every month.
steps: Adaeze chooses a calm Saturday morning and starts gently: 'I feel anxious about our savings when large amounts go out without us planning. Can we sit down with the numbers together?'
Tunde explains the need behind his position: as the first son, supporting his brothers' school fees matters deeply to him and to his late father's memory.
Adaeze shares hers: security for their own children and an emergency fund.
They write their monthly income (for example, N650,000 combined, approximate) and agree a fixed family-support amount of N80,000 per month, plus N50,000 into savings first.
They agree to review it every 3 months and to discuss any extra request above N20,000 together first.
blocks.result: The difference in values remains, but the monthly fight stops because they have a shared plan that respects both needs.

blocks.text: Everyday habits that protect a marriage

items: Turn towards bids: answer when your partner shares something, even briefly.
Say thank you for ordinary things: cooking, fixing the generator, school runs.
Spend 20 minutes a day talking about something other than bills and children.
Share the load at home openly; unspoken resentment about chores builds up.
Keep private disagreements private, not in front of relatives or on social media.

blocks.title: When it is not safe
blocks.text: Communication tools are for relationships where both people are safe. Hitting, threats, forced sex, controlling all the money, cutting you off from family, or constant insults are abuse, not a communication problem. You deserve safety. Reach out to trusted family, a faith leader, a lawyer, the police or an organisation that supports women. In Nigeria, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 provides legal protection against domestic violence.

Couples counselling, through a trained counsellor or a well-prepared faith-based marriage counsellor, can help when the same arguments keep repeating. Seeking help early, before resentment hardens, is a sign of commitment, not failure.

If you are single, widowed or separated, these skills still apply: to a future partnership, to co-parenting with a former partner, and to close relationships with siblings and friends. Co-parenting in particular goes better when both parents keep conversations about the children calm, brief and focused on the children's needs rather than on old hurts.

takeaways: Build love maps by asking about your partner's inner world.
Start gently, take breaks when flooded, and accept repair attempts.
Many conflicts are lasting differences: understand the need behind each side.
Abuse is a safety issue, not a communication issue; seek help.

activity.title: Love map and conflict plan
steps: Ask your partner (or a close family member, if you are single) two of the love map questions and write their answers.
Identify one recurring disagreement and decide if it is solvable or a lasting difference.
Write the need or dream you think sits behind each person's position.
Plan a calm time to talk and write your gentle start-up sentence.
activity.evidence: Love map notes, your solvable/lasting analysis and your gentle start-up sentence.

lessons.title: Leading with EQ in your community
objectives: Describe Goleman's six leadership styles and when each fits
Run a group meeting where everyone feels heard
Mediate a quarrel between two members using a simple process
Manage your own emotions under public pressure

blocks.text: Many women lead without a formal title: as a women's group chair, a cooperative secretary, a church or mosque coordinator, a market association leader, a school PTA member or a family elder. Leading people means handling their emotions as well as tasks. Groups do better when the leader stays calm, listens well and treats people fairly.

blocks.name: team-spirit
blocks.alt: A group of people celebrating together
blocks.caption: A leader's mood spreads through the group, for better or for worse.

blocks.text: Six leadership styles

In a well-known Harvard Business Review article, *Leadership That Gets Results* (2000), Goleman described six leadership styles, each drawing on different emotional intelligence skills. Good leaders switch between them depending on the situation.

head: Style
In one phrase
When it fits
rows: A real emergency only, such as a fire or safety threat
When the group needs a clear new direction
To heal rifts or support members through hard times
To build agreement and get good ideas from members
With a skilled, motivated team for a short push; overuse burns people out
To help individual members grow their skills

blocks.text: Running a meeting where people feel heard

items: Share a short agenda in the WhatsApp group a day before, so quieter members can prepare.
Open with a quick round: each person says one word about how they are or one good thing from the week.
For each decision, invite views from people who have not yet spoken: 'Mama Uche, what do you think?'
Summarise what you heard before deciding: 'So most of us prefer the 15th, but two members cannot make it. Can we...'
End by thanking people by name for specific contributions.

blocks.text: Mediating a quarrel

blocks.title: Five steps to mediate
items: Meet privately, set rules
Each tells their side
Reflect feelings and needs
Find shared goals
Agree clear next steps
blocks.caption: A calm, fair process helps both people feel respected.

blocks.title: Worked example: the cooperative contribution dispute
blocks.context: For example, Folake chairs a 20-member women's thrift cooperative in Ilorin. Two members, Mama Sade and Kafayat, quarrel publicly in the WhatsApp group: Kafayat says Mama Sade collected her payout early and has missed two contributions of N10,000 each (approximate).
steps: Folake posts in the group: 'Let us not discuss this here. I will meet both of you on Saturday.' She takes the conversation out of public view.
At the meeting she sets rules: one person speaks at a time, no insults.
Each tells her side. Folake reflects: 'Kafayat, you feel it is unfair because you have paid every week. Mama Sade, you are embarrassed because your shop was closed for a month after flooding.'
Shared goal: both want the cooperative to survive and stay trusted.
Agreement: Mama Sade pays the N20,000 in four weekly instalments of N5,000, recorded by the treasurer. Folake proposes a clear written rule for missed payments at the next meeting.
blocks.result: The group calms down, the missing money is repaid within a month, and the new written rule prevents future quarrels.

blocks.text: Staying steady under public pressure

items: Do not reply to provocation in a group chat while angry. Wait, then reply briefly and calmly, or move the conversation to private.
Separate the person from the problem: criticise ideas and actions, never someone's family or character.
Admit mistakes openly. A leader who says 'I got that wrong, here is how I will fix it' builds trust.
Protect confidentiality: what members share privately should not become gossip.

blocks.title: Lead by example
blocks.text: Members copy the leader. If you greet people warmly, listen without interrupting and stay calm during disagreements, the group slowly does the same.
Motivating volunteers

Most community groups run on volunteers, who give their time without pay. People stay involved when they feel valued, see that their work makes a difference, and have some say in decisions. A short personal thank-you, sharing results ('Our ajo helped 6 members restock this year'), and asking for ideas rather than only giving orders all draw on emotional intelligence.

items: Match tasks to people's strengths and interests, and ask before assigning.
Notice when someone is overloaded and offer to share their task.
Celebrate milestones together, even with something small like a shared meal.
When someone steps back, ask privately and kindly what has changed, instead of complaining about them in the group.

blocks.text: Remember that your own wellbeing matters as a leader. Leaders who are exhausted find it much harder to stay patient. Share responsibilities, train a deputy, and take breaks so that you can lead well for the long term.

takeaways: Goleman's six styles: switch between them to fit the situation.
Make quieter members heard with agendas, rounds and direct invitations.
Mediate privately: rules, both sides, reflect, shared goals, clear agreement.
Stay calm in public, admit mistakes and protect confidentiality.

activity.title: Community leadership practice
steps: Choose a group you belong to (family, cooperative, church, mosque, school, work).
Identify which leadership style you use most and one you could use more.
Plan your next meeting or group conversation using the five steps for being heard.
Write a short mediation plan for a real or likely conflict in the group.
activity.evidence: Your meeting plan and mediation plan, with a note on which leadership style you practised.

lessons.title: Your 30-day plan to keep growing
objectives: Review your progress since the start of the course
Choose two EI skills to focus on next
Build a 30-day practice plan with daily and weekly habits
Use feedback from others to track your growth

blocks.text: Emotional intelligence is not something you finish. Like physical fitness, it grows with regular practice and fades without it. In this final lesson you will look back at how far you have come, decide what to work on next, and make a simple plan you can follow for the next 30 days.

blocks.name: growing
blocks.alt: A person watering a growing plant
blocks.caption: Small daily practice is what makes emotional skills grow.

blocks.text: Step 1: Look back

Find the page from Lesson 1.1 where you scored yourself on Goleman's five areas. Score yourself again today, from 1 to 5. Then look at your logs and notes from the activities: your mood log, trigger log, anger ladder, resilience plan and conversation notes. Ask yourself: what has changed? Where do I still struggle?
Step 2: Ask for feedback
We often see ourselves differently from how others see us. Ask two or three people you trust to answer honestly. Thank them, and do not argue with what they say.

items: 'What is one thing I do well when I am under pressure?'
'What is one thing I could do better when I am upset?'
'Have you noticed any change in how I handle things recently?'

blocks.text: Step 3: Choose two focus skills
Choose only two skills, one about yourself (self-awareness, self-regulation or motivation) and one about others (empathy or social skills). Trying to change everything at once usually fails.

blocks.title: Your 30-day plan
items: Week 1: notice and log
Week 2: one tool daily
Week 3: harder situations
Week 4: review and feedback
blocks.caption: Each week builds on the one before, from awareness to confident practice.

blocks.text: Step 4: Build your plan

head: Week
Daily habit (5 to 10 minutes)
Weekly challenge
rows: Three mood checks a day with zone and feeling word
Log every strong reaction for the week
Box breathing every morning; STOP once a day
Use one 'I' statement in a real conversation
Have one gentle start-up conversation you have been avoiding
Reflective listening in one conversation a day
Ask two people for feedback; re-score yourself

blocks.title: Worked example: Esther's plan
blocks.context: For example, Esther, a nurse and mother of two in Jos, re-scores herself. Self-awareness has gone from 2 to 4, but self-regulation is still 2, and her sister says she 'goes quiet and sulks' after disagreements.
steps: Focus skill 1 (self): self-regulation, especially at the end of night shifts.
Focus skill 2 (others): social skills, especially speaking up instead of stonewalling.
Daily habit: 4 rounds of box breathing in the car before entering the house after each shift.
Weekly challenge: after any disagreement, return within 2 hours and say one 'I feel... I need...' sentence.
Tracking: a simple tick chart on her phone, with a weekly score from 1 to 5 for each skill.
blocks.result: After 30 days her self-regulation score is 3, and her husband notices she comes home calmer. She plans a second 30 days focused on the same two skills.

blocks.text: Keep learning

items: Read: Daniel Goleman's *Emotional Intelligence*, and John Gottman's books on relationships and parenting.
Use free tools: the WHO guide *Doing What Matters in Times of Stress*, and the Mood Meter idea from the Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence.
Practise with others: start a small EI practice circle in your WODDI or women's group, sharing one tool each week.
Seek professional support when needed: a counsellor or psychologist can help with deeper patterns.

blocks.title: Progress, not perfection
blocks.text: You will still have bad days, especially when tired, ill or under pressure. Growth shows up as recovering faster and repairing sooner. Celebrate small wins.
Common obstacles and what to do

head: Obstacle
What to try
rows: Attach the habit to something you already do daily, such as breathing after morning prayers or while the kettle boils.
Repair, note the trigger in your log, and start again tomorrow. One slip does not erase your progress.
Focus on your own responses. Often others soften over time when you stay calm and respectful.
Most tools take under 5 minutes. Even one mood check a day keeps the skill alive.

blocks.text: Keep your notebook from this course. It is a record of your growth and a toolkit you can return to whenever life becomes difficult. Many people find it useful to repeat the 30-day plan two or three times a year, especially before or after big life changes such as a new job, a new baby, a move or a bereavement.
Finally, share what you have learned. Teaching a tool to your children, your sister or your group helps you remember it, and spreads the benefits through your family and community.

takeaways: Emotional intelligence grows with regular practice and fades without it.
Re-score yourself and ask trusted people for honest feedback.
Focus on two skills at a time: one about you, one about others.
A 30-day plan of small daily habits and weekly challenges makes change stick.

activity.title: Write your 30-day plan
steps: Re-score yourself on Goleman's five areas and compare with Lesson 1.1.
Ask 2 trusted people the three feedback questions and write their answers.
Choose your two focus skills.
Fill in a 4-week table with one daily habit and one weekly challenge per week.
Put a reminder in your phone for day 30 to review.
activity.evidence: Your before-and-after scores, feedback notes, and a completed 30-day plan table.

quiz.q: A customer shouts that her order is late. Following LAST, what should the seller do first?
options: Explain that the delay was the supplier's fault
Listen without interrupting and reflect back what happened
quiz.explain: LAST starts with Listen. Customers calm down when they feel heard, which makes solving the problem easier.

quiz.q: Which feedback follows the SBI model?
options: You are always rude to customers.
At Monday's market (S), you raised your voice at the woman returning the bag (B). She left upset and told others nearby (I). What happened?
quiz.explain: It names the situation, the specific behaviour and its impact, then invites the person's view.

quiz.q: Kemi and her husband keep arguing about visiting his family every weekend. He values family closeness; she needs rest. According to Gottman, what kind of problem is this most likely to be?
options: A solvable problem with one right answer
A perpetual problem rooted in different needs, best handled by understanding both and finding a workable compromise
A sign the marriage will fail
quiz.explain: Ongoing differences in values or needs are perpetual problems. The aim is understanding and compromise, not winning.

quiz.q: Two cooperative members start quarrelling in the group WhatsApp. What should an emotionally intelligent chair do first?
options: Post her own opinion of who is right
Move the discussion to a private meeting with both
Ignore it and hope it stops
quiz.explain: Taking the conflict out of public view lowers the heat and allows a fair mediation process.

quiz.q: Bisi wants to improve her EI. Which plan is most likely to work?
options: Change all five areas at once this week
Pick two focus skills, practise a daily habit and review after 30 days
Read one book and stop there
Wait until she feels more motivated
quiz.explain: Focusing on two skills with small daily habits and a review point is far more realistic than changing everything at once.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is part of Goleman's five areas of emotional intelligence?
finalQuiz.explain: Goleman's five areas are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

finalQuiz.q: Ruth feels calm, content and a little sleepy after Sunday lunch. Which Mood Meter zone is she in?
finalQuiz.explain: Low energy and pleasant feelings belong in the green zone.

finalQuiz.q: Ada's colleague walks past without greeting her. Ada thinks, 'She hates me.' What is the best question to ask herself?
options: How can I get back at her?
finalQuiz.explain: Looking for other explanations challenges mind-reading. The colleague may simply be distracted or worried.

finalQuiz.q: Grace's trigger log shows most outbursts happen late at night when she has not eaten since lunch. What does HALT suggest?
options: She should avoid all people at night
Hunger and tiredness are making ordinary problems feel bigger, so she should plan food and rest
finalQuiz.explain: HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) explains this pattern. Basic needs come first.

finalQuiz.q: Which breathing pattern describes box breathing?
options: Breathe as fast as possible for one minute
Hold your breath as long as you can
finalQuiz.explain: Box breathing uses four equal counts of 4: in, hold, out, hold. A long, slow out-breath helps calm the body.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi is at level 8 on her anger ladder during an argument with her husband. What is the best step?
options: Keep talking until it is resolved
Say, 'I need 20 minutes to calm down, let's talk at 8pm,' and take a time-out
Raise her voice so he understands
finalQuiz.explain: At high anger levels, a time-out with a clear return time is best. Silence for days becomes stonewalling.

finalQuiz.q: A friend has had low mood almost every day for a month, cannot sleep, and says she feels hopeless. What should you do?
options: Tell her to cheer up and count her blessings
Encourage her to see a doctor or mental health professional, and stay with her if she feels unsafe
Wait another month to see if it passes
finalQuiz.explain: Lasting low mood and hopelessness are signs to seek professional help. Never share medicine; if she is unsafe, help her get urgent care.

finalQuiz.q: Which response shows empathy rather than sympathy?
options: At least you have other children.
That sounds so painful. I'm here with you.
I know exactly how you feel, the same happened to me but worse.
finalQuiz.explain: Empathy names the feeling and offers connection. 'At least' and one-upping close the conversation.

finalQuiz.q: In many Nigerian families, a young person avoids looking an elder in the eye. What does this usually show?
finalQuiz.explain: Cues must be read in cultural context. Lowered eyes towards elders are often a sign of respect.

finalQuiz.q: What is the antidote to defensiveness in Gottman's Four Horsemen?
options: Taking responsibility, even for part of the problem
finalQuiz.explain: Taking responsibility ('You're right, I forgot, I'm sorry') is the antidote to defensiveness. Appreciation is the antidote to contempt.

finalQuiz.q: A 4-year-old cries because he cannot have a sweet before dinner. Which response follows emotion coaching?
options: Okay, take the sweet so you stop crying.
You really wanted that sweet, you feel sad. We can have it after dinner. Let's choose which one together.
finalQuiz.explain: Validate and name the feeling, keep the limit, and solve the problem together.

finalQuiz.q: Patience receives an angry message calling her a scammer because one item arrived broken. What should she do first?
options: Pause to calm herself, then listen and reflect the customer's complaint
finalQuiz.explain: Regulate first (STOP), then use LAST, starting with listening. This protects her reputation and the customer relationship.

capstone.title: My Emotional Intelligence Practice Portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a personal portfolio that shows how you have applied emotional intelligence to real situations at home, at work and in your community over the course, ending with your 30-day growth plan.
steps: Collect your starting self-scores (Lesson 1.1), 5-day mood log and 7-day trigger log with your trigger plan.
Add your regulation evidence: the 7-day STOP and breathing chart, your anger ladder and your resilience plan.
Add your relationship evidence: notes from three reflective conversations, one gentle start-up conversation and one emotion-coaching record.
Add your applied evidence: a LAST script or SBI feedback from work, and a meeting or mediation plan from a group you belong to.
Write a one-page reflection: what has changed, what feedback you received, and what you still find hard.
Attach your 30-day plan with your two focus skills.
evidence: Before and after scores on Goleman's five areas
Mood log and trigger log with a trigger plan
At least five written STOP notes
One emotion-coaching or gentle start-up record
One work or community EQ plan (LAST, SBI or mediation)
